prompt: A brigade commander in Mindanao wants a force that attacks mounted in protected vehicles, combines fire and maneuver at the decisive time and place, and may also be tasked with ISO in peacetime. Which assessment of armor is accurate?
options: Armor fights mounted in armor-protected vehicles and uses controlled fire and maneuver, but it is barred from ISO in peacetime
Armor fights as a pure tank force without other arms, relies on shock effect alone, and conducts ISO only when attached
Armor fights mounted in armor-protected vehicles, uses controlled fire and maneuver, and may conduct ISO when higher HQ requires
Armor fights from protected static positions, relies on massed indirect fire, and conducts ISO only during wartime
explanation: Page 13 defines armor as a combined arms force fighting mounted in armor-protected vehicles, conducting operations by fire and maneuver combined and controlled; page 14 says it may also conduct ISO, independently or in a task force, in peacetime as required by higher headquarters.

prompt: A staff assigns three missions: (1) reconnaissance, surveillance and security; (2) neutralize the enemy by fire, maneuver and shock effect; (3) close with the enemy to destroy or capture him. Which units match, in order?
options: Tank, cavalry, mechanized infantry
Mechanized infantry, tank, cavalry
Cavalry, mechanized infantry, tank
Cavalry, tank, mechanized infantry
explanation: Pages 16-18 give these three missions.

prompt: An S3 argues that armor operations succeed through shock effect alone. Which flaw does the lesson expose?
options: Shock effect is not part of the armor mission at all; armor relies only on dismounted fire and maneuver to win
Armor operations depend mainly on armor protection, so firepower, mobility and shock effect are all secondary
Shock effect belongs only to cavalry, so tanks and mechanized infantry should rely on fire and maneuver alone
Shock effect works only with fire and maneuver, combined and controlled, and in coordination with other arms
explanation: Page 13 says armor operations are conducted by fire and maneuver, combined and controlled to create a preponderance of combat power; page 14 says armor neutralizes the enemy by fire, maneuver and shock effect in coordination with other arms.

prompt: After an exercise, a Philippine Army armor company is scored: crews survived small arms and machine gun fire, the radio net failed during maneuver, and the vehicles kept pace over varied terrain. Which assessment fits the lesson?
options: Armor protection was degraded, intensive and flexible communication held, and mobility held
Armor protection held, intensive and flexible communication was degraded, and mobility held
Armor protection held, intensive and flexible communication held, and mobility was degraded
Armor protection and mobility were degraded, while intensive and flexible communication held
explanation: Page 20 names all three characteristics.

prompt: A planner links vehicle features to characteristics: the 25 mm cannon, the amphibious M113A2 hull, and Level 4 ballistic protection on the Sabrah. Which linkage is correct?
options: Mobility, firepower, armor protection
Armor protection, mobility, firepower
Firepower, armor protection, mobility
Firepower, mobility, armor protection
explanation: Pages 20, 73, 75 and 82 support this linkage.

prompt: A mechanized infantry platoon has 1 officer and 37 enlisted; the HQ has 1 officer and 10 enlisted and the three squads are equal. How many enlisted are in each squad, and how many AIFVs does the platoon use?
options: 12 enlisted per squad; three AIFVs
9 enlisted per squad; four AIFVs
10 enlisted per squad; four AIFVs
9 enlisted per squad; three AIFVs
explanation: Page 25 gives 37 - 10 = 27, or 9 per squad; page 27 gives four AIFVs.

prompt: During a dismount near an enemy-held barangay, a Philippine Army squad's dismount team moves into a ditch while the AIFV driver waits to be told where to position the vehicle. The carrier team leader and the squad leader each assume the other will decide. Per the dismounting SOPs, who is responsible?
options: The squad leader or platoon leader, who answers for both the dismount team's maneuver and the AV's position
The carrier team leader, who places the AV, while the squad leader controls only the dismount team's maneuver
The driver, who positions the AV on his own initiative, since speed is of the essence during the dismount
The company first sergeant, as resource manager, who positions all AVs while the squad leaders maneuver
explanation: Page 31 says the SL or PL is responsible for both the maneuver of the dismount team and the positioning of the AV. The first sergeant appears in the lesson only as a possible resource manager in planning (page 69).

prompt: A Philippine Army mechanized infantry company commander must know his dismounted strength. Each squad has 9 enlisted, and each squad's carrier team is the normal three-man crew that stays with the AIFV. Counting only the squads, how many soldiers dismount across the company's three platoons?
options: 18, since six soldiers in each of the three squads dismount
81, since every squad member dismounts and leaves the AIFV
54, since six of nine enlisted dismount in each of nine squads
72, since only the driver stays and eight soldiers per squad dismount
explanation: Page 25 gives three squads of 9 enlisted per platoon and page 24 three platoons per company, or nine squads. Page 26 says the carrier team is normally the carrier team leader, gunner and driver, so six per squad dismount: 9 x 6 = 54. Eighteen is the count for one platoon only.

prompt: A platoon must assault unprepared, suppressed defenses, infiltrate along a trail vehicles cannot use, and fix the enemy so tanks can maneuver. Which allocation matches the lesson?
options: Assault dismounted; infiltrate mounted; fix mounted
Assault mounted; infiltrate and fix dismounted
Assault, infiltrate and fix all mounted
Assault, infiltrate and fix all dismounted
explanation: Pages 28-29 list the mounted and dismounted capabilities.

prompt: Enemy mortars range the only road while AIFVs halt so squads can dismount. Which limitations combine here?
options: AVs are restricted to certain avenues, infantry need time to dismount, and dismounted infantry are vulnerable to indirect fire
AIFVs are more vulnerable than tanks, AVs are restricted to certain avenues, and the infantry are safe once they dismount
AVs may use any avenue of approach, infantry need sufficient time to dismount, and small arms fire is the only risk to them
AIFVs and APCs are as protected as tanks, so the halt is safe, but dismounted infantry are vulnerable to indirect fire
explanation: Page 30 lists that AVs are restricted to certain avenues of approach, infantrymen need sufficient time to mount and dismount, and dismounted infantrymen are vulnerable to small arms and indirect fire; it also says AIFVs and APCs are more vulnerable than tanks.

prompt: A commander says mechanized infantry are tanks with legs and will lead an assault against enemy tanks. Which flaw does the lesson show?
options: Mechanized infantry may lead because mounted AIFVs can destroy light armor vehicles and maneuver with tanks
Mechanized infantry can be used against tank units if the infantry dismount and fix the enemy for the assault
Mechanized infantry cannot be used against tank units, and AIFVs and APCs are more vulnerable than tanks
Mechanized infantry lack the firepower to support tanks, so they should be kept out of every armored attack
explanation: Page 69 says mechanized infantry cannot be used against tank units, and page 30 says AIFVs and APCs are more vulnerable than tanks. Destroying light armor vehicles and maneuvering with tanks (page 28) do not extend to fighting tank units.

prompt: A squad dismounts left because terrain on the right is unfavorable, and fire opens from the right as it deploys. Which actions follow?
options: Return fire from the kill zone and stay beside the AV until it repositions, with the carrier team leader moving the AV
Dismount right toward the enemy fire to close with it, then let the driver reposition the AV once the contact ends
Remain mounted with the ramp closed until the fire ceases, then begin the dismount left drill under the platoon leader
React to contact on the right, extricate out of the kill zone, perform IAD, with the SL or PL positioning the AV
explanation: Pages 35-39 give the dismount left objectives under fire from the right: react to contact on the right, extricate out of the kill zone, and perform IAD after dismount procedures. Page 31 makes the SL or PL responsible for both the dismount team's maneuver and the AV's position.

prompt: A squad remounts from the right while under fire from the left. Which actions comply with the SOPs?
options: Rush the door together, keep weapons loaded with muzzles up inside, and close the ramp after the last soldier
Provide cover while others mount, avoid piling at the door, move in one at a time, clear weapons and muzzles down
Wait until the enemy fire stops, then have riders climb on top of the AV to watch the left flank during the move
Board in the same order the squad dismounted, take cover behind the AV, then mount when the cover team is ready
explanation: Page 45 lists the mounting SOPs; page 49 shows mounting from the right under fire from the left. Page 31 forbids riders on top and hiding behind an AV, and says the first to dismount is the last to mount.

prompt: Eight soldiers dismounted in order 1 through 8 and must remount under fire. Which sequence follows the SOPs?
options: Soldier 8 mounts first and soldier 1 last, one at a time, with cover provided
Soldier 1 mounts first and soldier 8 last, in a single rush to keep up speed
All eight mount at once in any order, since speed is of the essence under fire
Soldier 1 mounts first and soldier 8 last, one at a time, with cover provided
explanation: Page 31 says the first to dismount is the last to mount and vice versa; page 45 says to provide cover while others mount and to move inside one at a time.

prompt: A brigade commander gives a cavalry troop a zone reconnaissance as flank guard while keeping the main body concentrated for the decisive point. Which fundamentals support this?
options: Main effort, since cavalry attacks to overrun prepared defenses and so frees the main body to stay in reserve
Rear security and resupply of the main body, so the brigade's combat power can be spread along its whole flank
Economy of force, eyes and ears for situational awareness, and concentration of combat power at the decisive point
Reserve and counterattack roles, since cavalry must first be reinforced before it can operate as a flank guard
explanation: Page 53 calls cavalry the commander's eyes and ears and says it helps him concentrate superior combat power at the decisive time and point; page 54 describes its economy of force role; page 60 lists moving to contact as flank guard as zone reconnaissance, without reinforcement.

prompt: A separate cavalry troop with a light brigade must cover a flank through dense forest, steep ridges and a major river, with a stretched supply line. Which statement fits the lesson?
options: It works for the division commander as a heavy unit, and dense forest and rivers do not restrict its mobility
It works for the brigade commander as a heavy unit, since separate troops are heavy whatever the brigade type
It works for the division commander as a light unit, and its light design keeps logistics requirements low
It works for the brigade commander as a light unit, and high logistics needs and restricted mobility limit it
explanation: Page 58 says the separate troop is part of a separate light or armored brigade, heavy or light according to the brigade, and operates for the brigade commander; page 61 lists high logistics requirements and terrain-restricted mobility.

prompt: In terrain suitable for cavalry, a Philippine Army brigade commander gives his cavalry squadron three tasks: attack to penetrate a prepared enemy strong point, hold a wide sector in an economy of force role without reinforcement during a delay, and move to contact as the advance covering force. Which assessment matches the lesson?
options: All three are cavalry capabilities, applying its inherent combined arms mobility, firepower and shock effect
Only the move to contact fits; armor may assault only unprepared, suppressed defenses, not prepared strong points
Only the attack and move to contact fit; an economy of force role in a delay needs the squadron to be reinforced
None fits; cavalry is limited to reconnaissance, surveillance and security and must avoid attacks and delays
explanation: Page 60 says that in suitable terrain cavalry can operate in economy of force without being reinforced in offensive, defensive or delay operations, move to contact as part of the advance covering force, and attack to overrun, penetrate or envelop prepared enemy defenses or strong points. Assaulting unprepared, suppressed defenses is a mounted mechanized infantry capability (page 28).

prompt: A tank company is attached to an infantry battalion for a theater deployment. Which arrangements does the lesson require?
options: Tanks deploy under their own strategic mobility, and infantry battalion trucks carry their Classes III, V and IX
Tanks deploy by air, and the infantry battalion supplies Classes III and V, since the FFSU handles only Class IX
Flatbeds for deployment, plus FFSU and division CSS support, since the infantry lacks transport for tank CSS
Flatbeds for deployment, and the infantry battalion's organic trucks for Classes III, V and IX once in theater
explanation: Page 67 says the tank depends on flatbeds for deployment; page 68 says tanks need FFSU and division CSS support because infantry units lack the organic transportation to support tank CSS needs, especially Classes III, V and IX.

prompt: A light tank must fight in extremely close terrain against infantry with anti-armor weapons and antitank mines. Which statement fits the lesson?
options: It lacks main battle tank protection, is vulnerable to anti-armor weapons and mines, and close terrain restricts it
It matches main battle tank protection and resists mines, but extremely close terrain restricts its mobility
It lacks main battle tank protection, but close terrain improves its firepower against infantry with anti-armor weapons
Its armor protects it from small arms, machine guns and anti-armor weapons, so only its mobility is restricted
explanation: Page 67 says the light tank lacks the protection of a main battle tank and that tanks are vulnerable to infantry with anti-armor weapons and antitank mines; page 68 says mobility and firepower are restricted in extremely close terrain.

prompt: A Philippine Army tank platoon in an SBF position overwatches a mechanized infantry company assaulting an objective. Enemy armored vehicles then appear on the flank. Which plan matches the lesson?
options: The mechanized infantry turn their AIFVs on the enemy armor, while the tanks keep firing on the objective from the SBF
The tanks engage the enemy armor, using a planned surface danger zone and direct fire control measures to protect the assault
The tanks withdraw from the SBF to avoid the enemy armor, and the cavalry is called forward to engage it instead
The tanks stay on the objective and leave the enemy armor to indirect fire, since tanks should not fight other armor
explanation: Page 71 lists SBF positions, surface danger zone and direct fire control measures as tank planning considerations and says tanks can be used against other tanks or any armored vehicle of the enemy. Pages 69 and 70 say mechanized infantry and cavalry cannot be used against tank units.

prompt: A task force commander gives four assignments. Which one violates the lesson's planning considerations?
options: The cavalry troop screens at a planned distance from the main body
The mechanized infantry company attacks the enemy tank company
The tank platoon occupies an SBF position with cover against enemy air
The mechanized infantry commander plans where to dismount on, before or after the objective
explanation: Page 69 says mechanized infantry cannot be used against tank units; the other assignments follow pages 69-71.

prompt: A staff matches considerations to units: Ex-O as resource manager and objective-to-combat-trains distance; indirect fire weapon support and distance from main body; surface danger zone and SBF positions. Which units, in order?
options: Cavalry, tank, mechanized infantry
Tank, mechanized infantry, cavalry
Mechanized infantry, cavalry, tank
Mechanized infantry, tank, cavalry
explanation: Pages 69-71 list the considerations per unit.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: A planner needs wheeled vehicles only for a road march. Which group contains only wheeled vehicles from the lesson?
options: M113A2 APC, Simba Fighting Vehicle and Guarani 6x6
Commando V-150S, Mounted Mortar System and Guarani 6x6
Commando V-150S, Simba Fighting Vehicle and Guarani 6x6
Commando V-150S, M113A2 APC (Ambulance) and Simba Fighting Vehicle
explanation: Pages 79, 80 and 83 describe the Commando V-150S and Simba as wheeled AFVs and the Guarani as a 6x6 wheeled APC. The M113A2 APC, its ambulance version and the Mounted Mortar System are listed as full tracked laying (pages 73, 77 and 78).

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: An enemy armored vehicle halts 3,200 m from a Philippine Army position held by a Sabrah light tank, an M113A2 IFV with the Unmanned Turret System, a Fire Support Vehicle and a Guarani APC. Which vehicle can engage it within the stated effective range of its main weapon?
options: The Sabrah light tank with its 105 mm main gun
The M113A2 UTS with its 25 mm Bush-Master cannon
The Fire Support Vehicle with its 76 mm L23A1 gun
The Guarani with its 12.7 mm heavy machine gun
explanation: Page 82 gives the Sabrah's 105 mm a combat effective range of 3,600 m. The UTS 25 mm reaches 3,000 m effective (page 75), the FSV 2,200 m by direct fire (its 5,000 m semi-direct figure is a maximum range, page 81), and the Guarani 1,830 m (page 83).

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: A commander needs casualty evacuation, 81/120 mm mortar fire, and 76 mm direct fire support. Which vehicles fit, in order?
options: Mounted Mortar System, M113A2 APC (ambulance), Fire Support Vehicle
Fire Support Vehicle, Mounted Mortar System, M113A2 APC (ambulance)
M113A2 APC (ambulance), Fire Support Vehicle, Mounted Mortar System
M113A2 APC (ambulance), Mounted Mortar System, Fire Support Vehicle
explanation: Pages 77, 78 and 81 describe these vehicles.
